definition: Physical computing involves interactive systems that can sense and respond to the world around them.
details: While this definition is broad enough to encompass systems such as smart automotive traffic control systems or factory automation processes, it is not commonly used to describe them. In a broader sense, physical computing is a creative framework for understanding human beings' relationship to the digital world. In practical use, the term most often describes handmade art, design or DIY hobby projects that use sensors and microcontrollers to translate analog input to a software system, and/or control electro-mechanical devices such as motors, servos, lighting or other hardware. Physical computing intersects the range of activities often referred to in academia and industry as electrical engineering, mechatronics, robotics, computer science, and especially embedded development.

explainer.lead: Physical computing involves interactive systems that can sense and respond to the world around them. It matters as a creative framework for understanding humans' relationship to the digital world, most often through handmade art, design or DIY projects.

tiers.eli5: It is building things with sensors and tiny computers so they react to the real world, like a lamp that turns on when you clap.
tiers.practitioner: Makers use sensors and microcontrollers to translate analog input to a software system and/or control physical output; a pitfall is assuming the broad definition covers industrial systems, which it is not commonly used to describe.
tiers.paperLevel: Physical computing covers interactive systems that sense and respond to their surroundings; the term is broad enough to include smart traffic control or factory automation but is not commonly used for them.

explainer.example: A DIY project uses a microcontroller and a sensor to turn on a light when motion is detected.
